# Polygraph — a polygraph for your state machine

Guide the user through a five-step, trace-driven consistency check. You (the
in-session assistant) do the intelligent parts — designing the contract,
instrumenting the code, capturing traces, and triaging findings. The bundled
scripts do the mechanical parts — building the prompt, generating specs,
replaying, and classifying.

> **Tell the user this up front, once.** Disclosure: Polygraph is experimental,
> not peer-reviewed, unproven technology — newly published and highly
> speculative. It is a *consistency check, not a proof*:
> a clean run means the code's observable behavior matches an independent
> reading of its source, nothing more. "Exhaustive" means exhaustive over the
> finite (action, data) domains the contract/module declares — data-dependent
> behavior beyond those representative values is unchecked, and that
> abstraction gap is not measured by any gate. Every finding is a lead to investigate by
> hand, not an established result. Do not present it as a guarantee, and do not
> let it be the only safeguard for correctness- or safety-critical code.

> **Prerequisite — real traces, or this is the wrong tool.** The trace corpus
> is not an input among others; it IS the verification. Part 1 (replay) checks
> the code's *captured behavior* against an independent reading of its source —
> with no real traces there is nothing to check, and hand-modeling both sides
> is grading your own homework (the model-check half then only tests whether
> your own model agrees with your own invariants). If the code cannot be run
> and instrumented — no way to execute it, no test doubles buildable, capture
> forbidden — say so and stop: recommend hand-written modeling (e.g. TLA+ from
> the spec) instead of Polygraph. Do not substitute synthetic traces derived
> from reading the source; they inherit every misreading the specs will make.

All scripts live under `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/`. Node ≥ 20 is required.
Generation needs `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and an explicit model (recommend
`opus-5`; on an API policy refusal retry with `opus-4.8` — per-step source of
truth: `RECOMMENDED_MODELS` in `scripts/models.mjs`; there is no default).
Replay and controls need no key.

**The artifact (v0.7):** by default the derived spec is a **SAM v2
strict-profile module** (`@cognitive-fab/sam-pattern` 2.2.0, vendored at
`scripts/vendor/sam-pattern.cjs`): named intents with per-intent schemas and
finite payload **domains** declared in a manifest, acceptors keyed by intent
name, every ignored action an observable `reject(reason)`, a sealed model
(no hidden state), and **explicit next-state (prime) semantics** (sam-lib
2.1, #25) — each acceptor is a TLA+-style next-state relation: `model` is the
frozen pre-state, writes go to the `next` draft
(`next.x = model.x + 1`), and every declared variable is either assigned or
named `unchanged(...)` per accepted step. This buys evidence bare-next could
not produce: a failing no-op window now says *why* the spec did nothing
(`rejected(reason)` / `identity-by-mutation` / `unhandled`), dead wiring is a
load-time error instead of a silent zero, statement order can no longer
change a transition's meaning, the checker's exploration domains come from
the module's own manifest, every check runs a determinism double-pass, and
the spec is mechanically transpilable to TLA+ (`--tla`). The original bare
`next(state, action, data)` artifact was REMOVED in 8.0.0: it is refused by the
prompt builder, the replayer, the checker, and the mutation control alike.
(2.0-form strict modules — acceptors
that write `model.x` directly — throw `SamShapeError` under 2.1: migrate
them, see sam-pattern's docs/MIGRATION.md.)

House rule (from sam-lib #29, fixed structurally in 2.0.0-alpha.2): never
rely on `instance({}).state()` — on machines whose primary control key is
`state` it returns data, not the method. The pipeline and the prompts use
`getState()`/`setState()` exclusively.

## Step 1 — Define the contract (do this WITH the user)

Produce a `contract.json` (schema and example under
`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/templates/`). Decide, by reading the code:

- **stateKeys** — the minimal observable-state fields the behavior depends on.
  Exclude display strings, timestamps, and IDs that do not drive transitions.
  The FIRST key is the primary control state.
- **actions** — the discrete events that step the machine, each with its data
  shape. Use the step boundary the code already has (a dispatch, a reducer
  action, one handled message).
- **initState**, **terminalStates**, and **specialRules** (guards / rewrites /
  special cases that live outside the main state table — these are the rules
  models most often miss, so flag them for extra trace coverage). A rule's
  name/note is DOCUMENTATION of why a branch behaves as it does — naming a
  rule does NOT make that branch a rejection. In the v2 pipeline each rule is
  CLASSIFIED against the captured corpus (n8n field study,
  `eval/FINDING-n8n-reject-no-write.md`: generations rejected every branch
  that carried a rule name until the prompt distinguished them): windows all
  no-op → rendered as a required `reject(name)`; windows change state →
  rendered as a named BEHAVIORAL rule the acceptor must perform; unexercised
  → decide-from-source. Name rules for behavioral branches freely — but give
  every rule trace coverage so it classifies from evidence.
- **dataDomain** — REQUIRED in the v2 default for every action with data
  fields: a finite list of representative payload values per field. It is the
  generation domain, the model-checking exploration domain, and the TLC
  transpilation domain; a gap blocks generation loudly (no silent exclusion).

State the **no-op rule** explicitly: an action arriving where the code ignores
it yields `post == pre`. This makes the replay total. In the v2 artifact the
spec makes that no-op *observable* — it must `reject(reason)`, never throw.
Every action that appears in the traces must be declared in the contract: the
strict module has no silent-unknown-action fallback (an undeclared action
classifies as a contract-error, which is what it is).

## Step 2 — Capture traces from the code (YOU run this, autonomously)

This is the heavy step, and it is yours to carry — not the user's. If the code
does not run in isolation, **build the test doubles or emulators needed to run
it** (the finixpos study's agent built a payment-terminal emulator and a
fault-injection proxy to do exactly this), instrument a copy, drive the
scenarios, and produce the corpus. Only escalate to the user for judgment calls:
whether the contract's observable state is right, and whether a double you built
faithfully matches the real dependency (the correlated-oracle risk — validate at
least one assumption against a real service/sandbox when one exists).

Instrument a **copy** of the code (keep the change as a diff/patch) to emit one
NDJSON record per step: `{"pre":{...},"action":"NAME","data":{...},"post":{...}}`.
Capture `pre` before any internal rewriting of the action, `post` after it
settles.

- For JS/TS, offer the helpers in `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/instrument/`:
  `withTracing` (wrap a `dispatch(action, data)`), `tapReducer` (a Redux-style
  reducer), `traceStep` (you already have pre/post), and `withSamTracing`
  (`scripts/instrument/sam-emitter.mjs`) for code built on the SAM pattern
  (`@cognitive-fab/sam-pattern`, optionally with `sam-fsm`) — it wraps the
  `component` config so every dispatch emits a window, no-ops included. For other
  languages, write a small emitter by hand following the same shape.
- **Check for an existing seam before writing one.** If the target already
  exposes a step listener / observer / middleware hook, register on it — that
  is a stable attachment point, unlike a patch that rots when the code moves.
  Code authored through this toolchain always has one
  (`docs/capture-ready.md`); code polygen wrote is captured with
  `withSamTracingV2(instance, file)` and needs no shim at all. Only instrument
  a copy when no seam exists. Do NOT reshape someone else's target to make
  capture easier — that changes the thing under audit. (If you are separately
  fixing or authoring code in that repo, `docs/capture-ready.md` is what to
  shape it toward.)
- **Capture by event subscription, never by polling.** Hook the target's own
  event/observer/callback surface (a dispatch wrapper, a reducer tap, the
  library's Observer mechanism) so every transition emits a window. Treat
  "sleep and poll the state" as a red flag for ANY transition that can resolve
  faster than the poll interval: in the hashicorp/raft field study
  (`eval/FINDING-raft-field-study.md`), polling every ~2 ms silently missed
  *every* Candidate occupancy because elections resolved faster than the poll
  — the corpus looked healthy and was structurally blind to a whole state.
- Drive scenarios, one trace file per scenario: the normal path, each failure
  class, races, and deliberate glitches (an action into a terminal state → a
  no-op window). Use existing test doubles or emulators.
- **Sanity-check coverage against the contract**: a state or special rule the
  contract declares but the corpus never visits is a capture bug until proven
  otherwise (too-coarse polling, a scenario you didn't drive) — not evidence
  the state is rare. Step 3's `mutate.mjs --all` makes this check mechanical:
  a zero-flip mutation names a rule no trace exercises.
- Then validate the corpus:
  `node ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/validate_corpus.mjs contract.json traces/`
  Fix any chaining or terminal-state problem before continuing (traces are
  ground truth). Give any special rule ≥3 windows or the validator warns.

## Step 3 — Controls FIRST (never skip)

Before involving the model, establish that the replay discriminates:

- **Positive control**: write a reference `next()` yourself by reading the code;
  it must score 100%. Replay it with:
  `node ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/verify.mjs --contract contract.json --traces traces/ --specs <dir-of-your-reference-specs>`
- **Negative control — scripted, one command** (this is the only step that
  proves the harness CAN fail; do not hand-edit spec copies):

  ```
  node ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/mutate.mjs \
    --spec reference.js --contract contract.json --traces traces/ --all
  ```

  This enumerates targeted mutations of the reference (guard negation,
  transition retarget, acceptor widening, field freeze — the same operators
  polynv's adequacy grade uses), applies each, and reports the windows that
  flip. Read the three outcomes:
  - *windows flipped* — the corpus discriminates that rule ✓;
  - *behaviorally EQUIVALENT* — no corpus could distinguish this mutant;
    discarded, not a problem;
  - *ZERO windows flipped* (exit 1) — a **corpus blind spot**: no captured
    trace exercises that rule, so a real regression there would replay clean.
    Capture a trace that drives it before trusting a clean run. This is the
    trace-side twin of the checker's FROZEN STATE KEY warning.

  `--list` shows the mutation ids; `--apply <id>` runs one.

## Step 4 — Generate and replay

Run the full loop:

```
node ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/verify.mjs \
  --contract contract.json --source path/to/source --traces traces/ \
  --model opus-5 --n 5 --out out/
```

This builds a derivation-mode prompt (it never describes per-state semantics),
generates N independent specs, replays each, and writes `out/findings.md` and
`out/findings.json`. Use `--n 3` or more; a single generation may omit a rule.
If the first pass hits the reject-as-annotation signature uniformly (every
live spec rejected ≥2 windows the code acted on), verify **auto-regenerates
once** with the offending branches called out and reports the second pass —
both spec sets are preserved (`specs/`, `specs_regen/`); `--no-auto-regen`
disables this.

If every window comes back `unscoreable-all`, the generations were empty — with
a reasoning model (e.g. `claude-opus-5`) the thinking block spent the token
budget before any answer. Add `--max-tokens 32000` (the default is already 32000;
only lower it deliberately).

If generation reports `refused by the API (category=...)`, that is a **policy**
outcome, not a transient one — retrying the identical prompt will not help.
This is a live risk for this tool specifically: every prompt it sends is
"here is code, here is how it might be wrong," which is also what exploit
research looks like, so a source file whose own comments describe a bug can
trip the classifier. Switch `--model` (it has been model-specific in practice:
on 2026-07-24 `claude-opus-5` refused two eval machines on the since-removed
bare-next prompt that `claude-opus-4-8` and `claude-sonnet-5` accepted), or configure a
fallback model.

## Step 4b — Model-check the spec against invariants (THE BUG-FINDER)

Replay (Step 4) only catches a bug when the derived spec DISAGREES with the code.
A faithful spec — which capable models produce on legible code — does not
disagree, so replay alone misses real bugs (measured: `eval/FINDING-faithful-reproduction.md`).
The half that actually finds bugs is iterating the spec against invariants.

- Write `invariants.mjs` WITH the user — rules encoding what the code *should*
  do (intent), not what it does. Export
  `{ stateInvariants: [{name, pred:(state)=>bool}], transitionInvariants: [{name, pred:(pre,action,data,post)=>bool}] }`.
  A predicate returns true when the rule holds. Aim these at the special rules
  and at the safety properties the code exists to enforce ("never publish without
  approval", "never charge without confirmation", "lock by N attempts").
- Provide a finite `dataDomain` in the contract for actions with data (or rely on
  the values observed in the traces).
- Run it (verify.mjs runs it automatically when an `invariants.mjs` sits beside
  the contract, or pass `--invariants`):
  `node ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/check.mjs --spec <mod.js> --contract contract.json --invariants invariants.mjs --traces traces/`
- A reachable violation is a **bug**, reported with the shortest counterexample
  path from init. A violation reached by ALL generated specs is a strong signal
  (every independent reading reaches the bad state). Walk the counterexample in
  the source.
- In the v2 default, exploration domains come from the module's own
  `manifest()` (no `buildDomain()` inference, so nothing is silently excluded)
  and every check runs a determinism double-pass — a `nondeterminism` finding
  means two identical explorations diverged (a clock/random read in the spec).
- Honest limits: exploration is bounded (report cap hits); and a hazard that
  depends on an EXTERNAL service (not in the observable state) is invisible to
  reachability — it needs a real sandbox probe, not a bigger search.
- Read the checker's structural warnings, they are findings about the CHECK
  itself: a **FROZEN STATE KEY** (a key no action changes — Part 2 is blind to
  behavior it gates; seed `--initial-states` with non-default values, or
  capture traces that vary it) and a **drift warning** (a key minting fresh
  states forever — the state space is likely unbounded in that key; abstract
  it in the contract or lower `--max-states`, and treat any clean verdict as
  covering an arbitrary prefix).

## Step 4c — TLC escalation (optional, `--tla`)

Add `--tla` to `verify.mjs` to escalate the winning live spec (most windows
passed; tie → first) from "bounded exploration says" to "TLC says": the spec
is mechanically transpiled to TLA+ (`out/tla/*.tla` + `.cfg`), state
invariants whose predicates stay inside the translatable subset are carried
along as TLA+ INVARIANTs, and TLC runs when a toolchain is available
(`POLYGRAPH_JAVA` or `java` on PATH, plus `POLYGRAPH_TLA_JAR` pointing at
`tla2tools.jar`). The findings report gains a "TLC escalation" subsection:
states generated/distinct, a per-invariant verdict table, counterexample
steps on violation, and every skipped invariant named with its reason
(transition invariants are skipped by kind; check.mjs still checks them in
JS). A missing toolchain is a note, not an error — the `.tla`/`.cfg` are
still written for running elsewhere. A transpiler refusal names the offending
construct: transpilability is a checkable property of the spec.

## Step 5 — Triage each disagreement (do this WITH the user)

`findings.md` classifies every non-consistent window:

- **code-finding / contract-error** (all specs disagree with the trace): either
  the code does something unexpected (a defect — open the source at that
  pre-state and action) or the observable-state contract omits a field that
  drives the transition (widen it and return to Step 2).
- **spec-error** (some specs pass, some fail): usually one generation missed a
  rule — but check the report's **spec agreement** line and the **split**
  column first. A lopsided split (4-vs-1) cuts both ways: several specs making
  the IDENTICAL mistake looks the same as one spec missing a rule, and in the
  raft field study the majority was wrong (4 of 5 collapsed two independently
  gated updates into one; the lone dissenter matched the hand control). Judge
  the minority against the source, not the vote count. Note *which* rule — it
  is typically a special case outside the main state table, and worth a code
  comment for the next reader.
- **unscoreable in all specs**: the generated modules did not load or lack the
  expected surface. Fix generation, not the code.

In the v2 default each finding row also carries a **step classification** per
live spec. `rejected(reason)` and `identity-by-mutation` are the two GOOD
no-op classes (the spec explicitly declined, or explicitly re-committed the
same state); `unhandled` — the spec neither acted nor rejected — is itself a
finding (usually a missing acceptor case, or a rule the code has that the
contract does not). A *uniform* rejection-reason on a code-finding window
usually means the contract took a side (a specialRule the corpus classified —
or an authored rule declaring a no-op) that the code did not — triage it as a
contract question first. Note the tension with auto-regeneration: the regen
trigger fires on this same signature and re-prompts toward the CODE's
behavior; if the contract deliberately declared those windows no-ops, the
first pass in `specs/` was the real signal — re-run with `--no-auto-regen`
before accepting the regenerated pass.
And a `rejected(...)` classification on windows where the TRACE changed state
(the report counts these as "REJECTED while the code ACTED") is the
**reject-as-annotation trap** when uniform: a generation computes the correct
`next.*` writes and then appends `reject(reason)` as a success label,
discarding its own work (hatchet field study — 5 of 5 specs, 0/19 → 19/19 by
deleting that one line). Inspect the specs for a trailing reject after
`next.*` writes before reading any of it as a code finding.

When every window is consistent across all specs, report it as exactly what it
is: the code's observable behavior matches an independent reading of its source.
To go further, propose invariants over the traces, or a hand-written model
checked against an explicit environment.

## Notes to carry into the work

- Traces are ground truth. Spec-vs-trace disagreement with a correct-looking
  spec is a code finding, not a bad window.
- If the source uses a framework, a generated spec may copy the framework's
  wiring instead of the module contract — the bare `next()` contract minimizes
  this; watch for `unscoreable-all`.
- If traces come from a mock/emulator written alongside the code, both may share
  a misunderstanding of a real dependency. Validate at least one assumption
  against the real service (e.g. a sandbox).
- The spec must be deterministic. Model timeouts and other time-driven behavior
  as explicit actions issued by the environment, never as a clock read.

## Provenance — why these two artifacts, and why v2 is the default

The design follows the SysMoBench paper's findings (and its v2 postscript).
The paper's data splits Polygraph's two roles: as a **replay oracle**, the
the (now removed) bare-next artifact plus one discipline sentence was the
best performer for
pure trace conformance — and the control showed it was the sentence, not the
structure, that carried the robustness. That sentence is kept **verbatim** in
the v2 prompts: "Acceptors must guard against invalid proposals (an action
that the implementation does not act on in the current state must be a no-op
via `reject(reason)`, NOT a throw)". As a **checkable substrate**, the v2
strict module is strictly stronger: schema-enforced wiring (no silent dead
specs), sealed model (no hidden state), observable rejection, manifest-
declared domains (closing the silent-exclusion gap), determinism checking,
and a mechanical path to TLC. Polygraph ships one artifact for both roles —
v2 — because the N-spec voting layer absorbs exactly the failure mode v2
gives up (occasional individual conformance misses) while v2 eliminates the
failure modes voting cannot absorb (dead specs, hidden state, vacuous
exploration).

Reference implementation and origin: the SysMoBench "finixpos" study at
<https://github.com/jdubray/SysMoBench-1>. (Lineage note: this repo's disk
name, `bare-next-verify`, records the original bare-next artifact; the repo
is not being renamed.)

# Polygraph

**Your tests check the paths you thought of. Polygraph checks the ones you didn't.**

Polygraph is a Claude Code plugin (and standalone CLI) that finds bugs in
**stateful code** — workflows, reducers, protocol handlers, checkout flows,
session managers — by exhaustively exploring every state the code can reach
over a finite, declared domain of actions and payloads, and flagging the
ones that break rules you care about, like *"a customer is never charged
twice."*

You don't need to know anything about formal verification to use it. You
write the rules as plain JavaScript predicates. The heavy lifting — deriving a
formal model of your code, exploring the state space, producing a shortest
path to each violation — is done for you.

> **Disclosure — read this first.** Polygraph is **experimental, not
> peer-reviewed, unproven technology.** It is a **consistency check, not a
> proof**: a clean run means the code's observable behavior matches an
> independent reading of its own source, and nothing more. "Exhaustive"
> always means exhaustive **over the finite (action, data) domains declared
> in the contract** — not over unbounded real-world data (see
> [What "exhaustive" means](#what-exhaustive-means--and-what-it-doesnt)).
> Every finding is a
> *lead to investigate by hand*, not an established result. Do not rely on it
> as your only safeguard for correctness- or safety-critical code.

## About

Polygraph is developed by Cognitive Fab LLC (<https://cognitivefab.com>). For
questions, commercial support, or collaboration, reach us at
<hello@cognitivefab.com>.

## Demos & write-ups

The **DAAO demo** — a Dual-Authorization Action Order machine taken end to end
through the method (author it, break it, catch it, version-gate it) — lives in
its own repo: [`cognitive-fab/polygraph-demo-daao`](https://github.com/cognitive-fab/polygraph-demo-daao).

Three articles walk the demos:

1. [DeepSeek wrote the code. A two-line prompt checked every reachable state.](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/deepseek-wrote-code-two-line-prompt-checked-every-reachable-d--k0zvf/) — auditing existing code with `/polygraph:verify`.
2. [polygen wrote the dual-authorization code](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/polygen-wrote-dual-authorization-code-jean-jacques-d--mckuc/) — authoring verified-from-birth code with polygen.
3. [You just changed the code of your state machine. Now what?](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/you-just-changed-code-your-state-machine-now-what-jean-jacques-d--suh3c/) — version-gating a change against the live fleet with polyvers.

## Why Polygraph

Unit tests execute the scenarios you wrote. A state machine of even modest
size has orders of magnitude more reachable states than any test suite
visits — and the bugs that hurt in production live in the combinations nobody
wrote a test for: a retry landing after a cancel, a timeout racing a
confirmation, an event arriving in a state where nobody expected it.

Polygraph attacks that gap in two ways:

- **Audit existing code** (`/polygraph:verify`). An LLM reads your source and
  writes an independent, executable specification of it — a second opinion on
  what the code does. Polygraph then (1) replays real execution traces
  against that spec to confirm it's faithful, and (2) **model-checks** it:
  starting from the initial state, it tries every action with every declared
  payload value, visits every state reachable that way, and reports any state that violates
  one of your rules — with the shortest sequence of actions that gets there.
  That counterexample path is a ready-made repro for the bug.

- **Author new code** (`polygen`). Give it a one-sentence feature description
  and it writes the state machine *and* its rules, model-checks its own
  output, repairs violations, and hands you code with a passing exhaustive
  check plus a generated regression trace corpus — verified from the moment
  it's written.

Real result: on a production SaaS subscription-billing machine, this method
independently corroborated a genuine double-charge bug
([`examples/case-study-subscription.md`](examples/case-study-subscription.md)).
In the controlled eval, replay alone found 0/5 seeded bugs — model checking
found 5/5, with counterexamples
([`eval/FINDING-faithful-reproduction.md`](eval/FINDING-faithful-reproduction.md)).

### Why not use TLA+ / Alloy / a model checker directly?

Those tools work — but you have to hand-translate your code into their
language and keep the translation current, which is why almost nobody does
it. Specifying even a small-to-midsize system is a multi-month effort, and
every code change invalidates the spec. Polygraph's bet is that an LLM can
produce that formal model *from your source* cheaply enough to rerun on every
change, and that replaying real traces against the model tells you whether to
trust it. You stay in JavaScript the whole time. (If you *do* want the real
thing, an optional `--tla` flag mechanically transpiles the winning spec to
TLA+ and runs TLC over it.)

This bet is no longer a fringe position — and the strongest evidence for it
comes from a project that is **ahead of Polygraph on the one axis the two
share**:

> **Specula: Scaling formal specifications for autonomous model checking of
> system code.** arXiv:2607.25333v2, August 2026.
> <https://github.com/specula-org/Specula> (Apache-2.0)

Specula is an agentic TLA+ pipeline standing on the same three legs Polygraph
does — spec generation, model checking, trace validation. Its paper reports
**249 bugs across 48 projects** (MongoDB, Etcd, ScyllaDB, GCC libgomp, LLVM
libomp) in seven languages and 2K–95K LoC: 207 previously unknown, 89
reported upstream, 68 confirmed and 24 fixed, at a median of $57 and 3.7
hours per system. 200 of the 249 surfaced through model checking; the rest
came out of code comprehension along the way. The convergent finding is the
one that matters: the LLM alone is not trustworthy, but an LLM *held
accountable by a model checker and trace validation* is a practical
bug-finder.

**On coverage, the two are closer than the languages suggest.** It is
tempting to read this as rigorous-TLA+ versus pragmatic-JS. That is not
where the difference lies. Specula builds a *reference model* of the system
at whatever abstraction its invariants require, then **projects** that model
into smaller scenario models — bounding how often an action can occur,
collapsing a multi-step protocol into one atomic step, forcing an ordering.
The projection is sound in the direction that matters: a violation found in
a projection is a violation in the reference model.

48	# Polygraph — a polygraph for your state machine
49	
50	Guide the user through a five-step, trace-driven consistency check. You (the
51	in-session assistant) do the intelligent parts — designing the contract,
52	instrumenting the code, capturing traces, and triaging findings. The bundled
53	scripts do the mechanical parts — building the prompt, generating specs,
54	replaying, and classifying.
55	
56	> **Tell the user this up front, once.** Disclosure: Polygraph is experimental,
57	> not peer-reviewed, unproven technology — newly published and highly
58	> speculative. It is a *consistency check, not a proof*:
59	> a clean run means the code's observable behavior matches an independent
60	> reading of its source, nothing more. "Exhaustive" means exhaustive over the
61	> finite (action, data) domains the contract/module declares — data-dependent
62	> behavior beyond those representative values is unchecked, and that
63	> abstraction gap is not measured by any gate. Every finding is a lead to investigate by
64	> hand, not an established result. Do not present it as a guarantee, and do not
65	> let it be the only safeguard for correctness- or safety-critical code.
66	
67	> **Prerequisite — real traces, or this is the wrong tool.** The trace corpus
68	> is not an input among others; it IS the verification. Part 1 (replay) checks
69	> the code's *captured behavior* against an independent reading of its source —
70	> with no real traces there is nothing to check, and hand-modeling both sides
71	> is grading your own homework (the model-check half then only tests whether
72	> your own model agrees with your own invariants). If the code cannot be run
73	> and instrumented — no way to execute it, no test doubles buildable, capture
74	> forbidden — say so and stop: recommend hand-written modeling (e.g. TLA+ from
75	> the spec) instead of Polygraph. Do not substitute synthetic traces derived
76	> from reading the source; they inherit every misreading the specs will make.

78	All scripts live under `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/`. Node ≥ 20 is required.
79	Generation needs `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and an explicit model (recommend

84	**The artifact (v0.7):** by default the derived spec is a **SAM v2
85	strict-profile module** (`@cognitive-fab/sam-pattern` 2.2.0, vendored at
86	`scripts/vendor/sam-pattern.cjs`): named intents with per-intent schemas and
87	finite payload **domains** declared in a manifest, acceptors keyed by intent
88	name, every ignored action an observable `reject(reason)`, a sealed model
89	(no hidden state), and **explicit next-state (prime) semantics** (sam-lib
90	2.1, #25) — each acceptor is a TLA+-style next-state relation: `model` is the
91	frozen pre-state, writes go to the `next` draft
92	(`next.x = model.x + 1`), and every declared variable is either assigned or
93	named `unchanged(...)` per accepted step. This buys evidence bare-next could
94	not produce: a failing no-op window now says *why* the spec did nothing
95	(`rejected(reason)` / `identity-by-mutation` / `unhandled`), dead wiring is a
96	load-time error instead of a silent zero, statement order can no longer
97	change a transition's meaning, the checker's exploration domains come from
98	the module's own manifest, every check runs a determinism double-pass, and
99	the spec is mechanically transpilable to TLA+ (`--tla`). The original bare
100	`next(state, action, data)` artifact was REMOVED in 8.0.0: it is refused by the
101	prompt builder, the replayer, the checker, and the mutation control alike.
102	(2.0-form strict modules — acceptors
103	that write `model.x` directly — throw `SamShapeError` under 2.1: migrate
104	them, see sam-pattern's docs/MIGRATION.md.)
105	
106	House rule (from sam-lib #29, fixed structurally in 2.0.0-alpha.2): never
107	rely on `instance({}).state()` — on machines whose primary control key is
108	`state` it returns data, not the method. The pipeline and the prompts use
109	`getState()`/`setState()` exclusively.

111	## Step 1 — Define the contract (do this WITH the user)
112	
113	Produce a `contract.json` (schema and example under
114	`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/templates/`). Decide, by reading the code:
115	
116	- **stateKeys** — the minimal observable-state fields the behavior depends on.
117	  Exclude display strings, timestamps, and IDs that do not drive transitions.
118	  The FIRST key is the primary control state.
119	- **actions** — the discrete events that step the machine, each with its data
120	  shape. Use the step boundary the code already has (a dispatch, a reducer
121	  action, one handled message).
122	- **initState**, **terminalStates**, and **specialRules** (guards / rewrites /
123	  special cases that live outside the main state table — these are the rules
124	  models most often miss, so flag them for extra trace coverage). A rule's
125	  name/note is DOCUMENTATION of why a branch behaves as it does — naming a
126	  rule does NOT make that branch a rejection. In the v2 pipeline each rule is
127	  CLASSIFIED against the captured corpus (n8n field study,
128	  `eval/FINDING-n8n-reject-no-write.md`: generations rejected every branch
129	  that carried a rule name until the prompt distinguished them): windows all
130	  no-op → rendered as a required `reject(name)`; windows change state →
131	  rendered as a named BEHAVIORAL rule the acceptor must perform; unexercised
132	  → decide-from-source. Name rules for behavioral branches freely — but give
133	  every rule trace coverage so it classifies from evidence.
134	- **dataDomain** — REQUIRED in the v2 default for every action with data
135	  fields: a finite list of representative payload values per field. It is the
136	  generation domain, the model-checking exploration domain, and the TLC
137	  transpilation domain; a gap blocks generation loudly (no silent exclusion).
138	
139	State the **no-op rule** explicitly: an action arriving where the code ignores
140	it yields `post == pre`. This makes the replay total. In the v2 artifact the
141	spec makes that no-op *observable* — it must `reject(reason)`, never throw.
142	Every action that appears in the traces must be declared in the contract: the
143	strict module has no silent-unknown-action fallback (an undeclared action
144	classifies as a contract-error, which is what it is).

146	## Step 2 — Capture traces from the code (YOU run this, autonomously)
147	
148	This is the heavy step, and it is yours to carry — not the user's. If the code
149	does not run in isolation, **build the test doubles or emulators needed to run
150	it** (the finixpos study's agent built a payment-terminal emulator and a
151	fault-injection proxy to do exactly this), instrument a copy, drive the
152	scenarios, and produce the corpus. Only escalate to the user for judgment calls:
153	whether the contract's observable state is right, and whether a double you built
154	faithfully matches the real dependency (the correlated-oracle risk — validate at
155	least one assumption against a real service/sandbox when one exists).
156	
157	Instrument a **copy** of the code (keep the change as a diff/patch) to emit one
158	NDJSON record per step: `{"pre":{...},"action":"NAME","data":{...},"post":{...}}`.
159	Capture `pre` before any internal rewriting of the action, `post` after it
160	settles.
161	
162	- For JS/TS, offer the helpers in `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/instrument/`:

172	  Code authored through this toolchain always has one

180	  event/observer/callback surface (a dispatch wrapper, a reducer tap, the

198	  ground truth). Give any special rule ≥3 windows or the validator warns.

200	## Step 3 — Controls FIRST (never skip)
201	
202	Before involving the model, establish that the replay discriminates:
203	
204	- **Positive control**: write a reference `next()` yourself by reading the code;
205	  it must score 100%. Replay it with:
206	  `node ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/verify.mjs --contract contract.json --traces traces/ --specs <dir-of-your-reference-specs>`
207	- **Negative control — scripted, one command** (this is the only step that
208	  proves the harness CAN fail; do not hand-edit spec copies):
209	
210	  ```
211	  node ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/mutate.mjs \
212	    --spec reference.js --contract contract.json --traces traces/ --all
213	  ```
214	
215	  This enumerates targeted mutations of the reference (guard negation,
216	  transition retarget, acceptor widening, field freeze — the same operators
217	  polynv's adequacy grade uses), applies each, and reports the windows that
218	  flip. Read the three outcomes:
219	  - *windows flipped* — the corpus discriminates that rule ✓;
220	  - *behaviorally EQUIVALENT* — no corpus could distinguish this mutant;
221	    discarded, not a problem;
222	  - *ZERO windows flipped* (exit 1) — a **corpus blind spot**: no captured
223	    trace exercises that rule, so a real regression there would replay clean.
224	    Capture a trace that drives it before trusting a clean run. This is the
225	    trace-side twin of the checker's FROZEN STATE KEY warning.
226	
227	  `--list` shows the mutation ids; `--apply <id>` runs one.

229	## Step 4 — Generate and replay
230	
231	Run the full loop:
232	
233	```
234	node ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/verify.mjs \
235	  --contract contract.json --source path/to/source --traces traces/ \
236	  --model opus-5 --n 5 --out out/
237	```
238	
239	This builds a derivation-mode prompt (it never describes per-state semantics),
240	generates N independent specs, replays each, and writes `out/findings.md` and
241	`out/findings.json`. Use `--n 3` or more; a single generation may omit a rule.
242	If the first pass hits the reject-as-annotation signature uniformly (every
243	live spec rejected ≥2 windows the code acted on), verify **auto-regenerates

245	both spec sets are preserved (`specs/`, `specs_regen/`); `--no-auto-regen`

248	If every window comes back `unscoreable-all`, the generations were empty — with
249	a reasoning model (e.g. `claude-opus-5`) the thinking block spent the token

253	If generation reports `refused by the API (category=...)`, that is a **policy**

263	## Step 4b — Model-check the spec against invariants (THE BUG-FINDER)
264	
265	Replay (Step 4) only catches a bug when the derived spec DISAGREES with the code.
266	A faithful spec — which capable models produce on legible code — does not
267	disagree, so replay alone misses real bugs (measured: `eval/FINDING-faithful-reproduction.md`).
268	The half that actually finds bugs is iterating the spec against invariants.
269	
270	- Write `invariants.mjs` WITH the user — rules encoding what the code *should*
271	  do (intent), not what it does. Export
272	  `{ stateInvariants: [{name, pred:(state)=>bool}], transitionInvariants: [{name, pred:(pre,action,data,post)=>bool}] }`.
273	  A predicate returns true when the rule holds. Aim these at the special rules
274	  and at the safety properties the code exists to enforce ("never publish without
275	  approval", "never charge without confirmation", "lock by N attempts").
276	- Provide a finite `dataDomain` in the contract for actions with data (or rely on
277	  the values observed in the traces).
278	- Run it (verify.mjs runs it automatically when an `invariants.mjs` sits beside
279	  the contract, or pass `--invariants`):
280	  `node ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/check.mjs --spec <mod.js> --contract contract.json --invariants invariants.mjs --traces traces/`
281	- A reachable violation is a **bug**, reported with the shortest counterexample
282	  path from init. A violation reached by ALL generated specs is a strong signal
283	  (every independent reading reaches the bad state). Walk the counterexample in
284	  the source.
285	- In the v2 default, exploration domains come from the module's own
286	  `manifest()` (no `buildDomain()` inference, so nothing is silently excluded)
287	  and every check runs a determinism double-pass — a `nondeterminism` finding
288	  means two identical explorations diverged (a clock/random read in the spec).
289	- Honest limits: exploration is bounded (report cap hits); and a hazard that
290	  depends on an EXTERNAL service (not in the observable state) is invisible to
291	  reachability — it needs a real sandbox probe, not a bigger search.
292	- Read the checker's structural warnings, they are findings about the CHECK
293	  itself: a **FROZEN STATE KEY** (a key no action changes — Part 2 is blind to
294	  behavior it gates; seed `--initial-states` with non-default values, or
295	  capture traces that vary it) and a **drift warning** (a key minting fresh
296	  states forever — the state space is likely unbounded in that key; abstract
297	  it in the contract or lower `--max-states`, and treat any clean verdict as
298	  covering an arbitrary prefix).
299	
300	## Step 4c — TLC escalation (optional, `--tla`)
301	
302	Add `--tla` to `verify.mjs` to escalate the winning live spec (most windows
303	passed; tie → first) from "bounded exploration says" to "TLC says": the spec
304	is mechanically transpiled to TLA+ (`out/tla/*.tla` + `.cfg`), state
305	invariants whose predicates stay inside the translatable subset are carried
306	along as TLA+ INVARIANTs, and TLC runs when a toolchain is available
307	(`POLYGRAPH_JAVA` or `java` on PATH, plus `POLYGRAPH_TLA_JAR` pointing at
308	`tla2tools.jar`). The findings report gains a "TLC escalation" subsection:
309	states generated/distinct, a per-invariant verdict table, counterexample
310	steps on violation, and every skipped invariant named with its reason
311	(transition invariants are skipped by kind; check.mjs still checks them in
312	JS). A missing toolchain is a note, not an error — the `.tla`/`.cfg` are
313	still written for running elsewhere. A transpiler refusal names the offending
314	construct: transpilability is a checkable property of the spec.
315	
316	## Step 5 — Triage each disagreement (do this WITH the user)
317	
318	`findings.md` classifies every non-consistent window:
319	
320	- **code-finding / contract-error** (all specs disagree with the trace): either
321	  the code does something unexpected (a defect — open the source at that
322	  pre-state and action) or the observable-state contract omits a field that
323	  drives the transition (widen it and return to Step 2).
324	- **spec-error** (some specs pass, some fail): usually one generation missed a
325	  rule — but check the report's **spec agreement** line and the **split**
326	  column first. A lopsided split (4-vs-1) cuts both ways: several specs making
327	  the IDENTICAL mistake looks the same as one spec missing a rule, and in the
328	  raft field study the majority was wrong (4 of 5 collapsed two independently
329	  gated updates into one; the lone dissenter matched the hand control). Judge
330	  the minority against the source, not the vote count. Note *which* rule — it
331	  is typically a special case outside the main state table, and worth a code
332	  comment for the next reader.
333	- **unscoreable in all specs**: the generated modules did not load or lack the
334	  expected surface. Fix generation, not the code.
335	
336	In the v2 default each finding row also carries a **step classification** per
337	live spec. `rejected(reason)` and `identity-by-mutation` are the two GOOD
338	no-op classes (the spec explicitly declined, or explicitly re-committed the
339	same state); `unhandled` — the spec neither acted nor rejected — is itself a
340	finding (usually a missing acceptor case, or a rule the code has that the
341	contract does not). A *uniform* rejection-reason on a code-finding window
342	usually means the contract took a side (a specialRule the corpus classified —
343	or an authored rule declaring a no-op) that the code did not — triage it as a
344	contract question first. Note the tension with auto-regeneration: the regen
345	trigger fires on this same signature and re-prompts toward the CODE's
346	behavior; if the contract deliberately declared those windows no-ops, the
347	first pass in `specs/` was the real signal — re-run with `--no-auto-regen`
348	before accepting the regenerated pass.
349	And a `rejected(...)` classification on windows where the TRACE changed state
350	(the report counts these as "REJECTED while the code ACTED") is the
351	**reject-as-annotation trap** when uniform: a generation computes the correct
352	`next.*` writes and then appends `reject(reason)` as a success label,
353	discarding its own work (hatchet field study — 5 of 5 specs, 0/19 → 19/19 by
354	deleting that one line). Inspect the specs for a trailing reject after
355	`next.*` writes before reading any of it as a code finding.
356	
357	When every window is consistent across all specs, report it as exactly what it
358	is: the code's observable behavior matches an independent reading of its source.
359	To go further, propose invariants over the traces, or a hand-written model
360	checked against an explicit environment.
361	
362	## Notes to carry into the work
363	
364	- Traces are ground truth. Spec-vs-trace disagreement with a correct-looking
365	  spec is a code finding, not a bad window.
366	- If the source uses a framework, a generated spec may copy the framework's
367	  wiring instead of the module contract — the bare `next()` contract minimizes
368	  this; watch for `unscoreable-all`.
369	- If traces come from a mock/emulator written alongside the code, both may share
370	  a misunderstanding of a real dependency. Validate at least one assumption
371	  against the real service (e.g. a sandbox).
372	- The spec must be deterministic. Model timeouts and other time-driven behavior
373	  as explicit actions issued by the environment, never as a clock read.
374	
375	## Provenance — why these two artifacts, and why v2 is the default
376	
377	The design follows the SysMoBench paper's findings (and its v2 postscript).
378	The paper's data splits Polygraph's two roles: as a **replay oracle**, the
379	the (now removed) bare-next artifact plus one discipline sentence was the
380	best performer for
381	pure trace conformance — and the control showed it was the sentence, not the
382	structure, that carried the robustness. That sentence is kept **verbatim** in
383	the v2 prompts: "Acceptors must guard against invalid proposals (an action
384	that the implementation does not act on in the current state must be a no-op
385	via `reject(reason)`, NOT a throw)". As a **checkable substrate**, the v2
386	strict module is strictly stronger: schema-enforced wiring (no silent dead
387	specs), sealed model (no hidden state), observable rejection, manifest-
388	declared domains (closing the silent-exclusion gap), determinism checking,
389	and a mechanical path to TLC. Polygraph ships one artifact for both roles —

403	# Polygraph
404	
405	**Your tests check the paths you thought of. Polygraph checks the ones you didn't.**
406	
407	Polygraph is a Claude Code plugin (and standalone CLI) that finds bugs in
408	**stateful code** — workflows, reducers, protocol handlers, checkout flows,
409	session managers — by exhaustively exploring every state the code can reach
410	over a finite, declared domain of actions and payloads, and flagging the
411	ones that break rules you care about, like *"a customer is never charged
412	twice."*
413	
414	You don't need to know anything about formal verification to use it. You
415	write the rules as plain JavaScript predicates. The heavy lifting — deriving a
416	formal model of your code, exploring the state space, producing a shortest
417	path to each violation — is done for you.
418	
419	> **Disclosure — read this first.** Polygraph is **experimental, not
420	> peer-reviewed, unproven technology.** It is a **consistency check, not a
421	> proof**: a clean run means the code's observable behavior matches an
422	> independent reading of its own source, and nothing more. "Exhaustive"
423	> always means exhaustive **over the finite (action, data) domains declared
424	> in the contract** — not over unbounded real-world data (see
425	> [What "exhaustive" means](#what-exhaustive-means--and-what-it-doesnt)).
426	> Every finding is a
427	> *lead to investigate by hand*, not an established result. Do not rely on it
428	> as your only safeguard for correctness- or safety-critical code.

448	## Why Polygraph
449	
450	Unit tests execute the scenarios you wrote. A state machine of even modest
451	size has orders of magnitude more reachable states than any test suite
452	visits — and the bugs that hurt in production live in the combinations nobody
453	wrote a test for: a retry landing after a cancel, a timeout racing a
454	confirmation, an event arriving in a state where nobody expected it.
455	
456	Polygraph attacks that gap in two ways:
457	
458	- **Audit existing code** (`/polygraph:verify`). An LLM reads your source and
459	  writes an independent, executable specification of it — a second opinion on
460	  what the code does. Polygraph then (1) replays real execution traces
461	  against that spec to confirm it's faithful, and (2) **model-checks** it:
462	  starting from the initial state, it tries every action with every declared
463	  payload value, visits every state reachable that way, and reports any state that violates
464	  one of your rules — with the shortest sequence of actions that gets there.
465	  That counterexample path is a ready-made repro for the bug.
466	
467	- **Author new code** (`polygen`). Give it a one-sentence feature description
468	  and it writes the state machine *and* its rules, model-checks its own
469	  output, repairs violations, and hands you code with a passing exhaustive
470	  check plus a generated regression trace corpus — verified from the moment
471	  it's written.
472	
473	Real result: on a production SaaS subscription-billing machine, this method
474	independently corroborated a genuine double-charge bug
475	([`examples/case-study-subscription.md`](examples/case-study-subscription.md)).
476	In the controlled eval, replay alone found 0/5 seeded bugs — model checking
477	found 5/5, with counterexamples
478	([`eval/FINDING-faithful-reproduction.md`](eval/FINDING-faithful-reproduction.md)).
479	
480	### Why not use TLA+ / Alloy / a model checker directly?
481	
482	Those tools work — but you have to hand-translate your code into their
483	language and keep the translation current, which is why almost nobody does
484	it. Specifying even a small-to-midsize system is a multi-month effort, and
485	every code change invalidates the spec. Polygraph's bet is that an LLM can
486	produce that formal model *from your source* cheaply enough to rerun on every
487	change, and that replaying real traces against the model tells you whether to
488	trust it. You stay in JavaScript the whole time. (If you *do* want the real
489	thing, an optional `--tla` flag mechanically transpiles the winning spec to
490	TLA+ and runs TLC over it.)
491	
492	This bet is no longer a fringe position — and the strongest evidence for it
493	comes from a project that is **ahead of Polygraph on the one axis the two
494	share**:
495	
496	> **Specula: Scaling formal specifications for autonomous model checking of
497	> system code.** arXiv:2607.25333v2, August 2026.
498	> <https://github.com/specula-org/Specula> (Apache-2.0)
499	
500	Specula is an agentic TLA+ pipeline standing on the same three legs Polygraph
501	does — spec generation, model checking, trace validation. Its paper reports
502	**249 bugs across 48 projects** (MongoDB, Etcd, ScyllaDB, GCC libgomp, LLVM
503	libomp) in seven languages and 2K–95K LoC: 207 previously unknown, 89
504	reported upstream, 68 confirmed and 24 fixed, at a median of $57 and 3.7
505	hours per system. 200 of the 249 surfaced through model checking; the rest
506	came out of code comprehension along the way. The convergent finding is the
507	one that matters: the LLM alone is not trustworthy, but an LLM *held
508	accountable by a model checker and trace validation* is a practical
509	bug-finder.
510	
511	**On coverage, the two are closer than the languages suggest.** It is
512	tempting to read this as rigorous-TLA+ versus pragmatic-JS. That is not
513	where the difference lies. Specula builds a *reference model* of the system
514	at whatever abstraction its invariants require, then **projects** that model
515	into smaller scenario models — bounding how often an action can occur,
516	collapsing a multi-step protocol into one atomic step, forcing an ordering.
517	The projection is sound in the direction that matters: a violation found in
518	a projection is a violation in the reference model. Polygraph enumerates a
519	finite (action, data) domain declared in the contract and visits every state
520	reachable over it. **Both make an unbounded space tractable by declaring an
521	abstraction, then search what is left close to exhaustively** — 93.5% of
522	Specula's model-checked bugs fall out of plain breadth-first search, at a
523	median counterexample of 9 steps. And neither measures the distance between
524	the declared abstraction and the real system. Their paper says so plainly:
525	
526	> "there is no formal guarantee that it models everything perfectly… A model
527	> can therefore remain inconsistent with the implementation in ways we did
528	> not catch, and a bug that depends on such a gap can remain undetected."
529	
530	That is the same caveat we give in
531	[What "exhaustive" means](#what-exhaustive-means--and-what-it-doesnt), from
532	a project with 249 bugs behind it. Read it as the shape of the field, not
533	as either project's weakness.
534	
535	Where Specula is ahead of Polygraph's audit engine, plainly:
536	
537	- **Its capture is engine-owned and repeatable.** Its agents instrument the
538	  target, and a replay harness verifies post-state agreement inside the
539	  pipeline, with a conformance repair loop. Polygraph's capture is owned by
540	  the agent per run (Step 2 of the skill), so the harness is not by default a
541	  committed, re-runnable artifact.
542	- **It reproduces bugs in the running system**, forcing the counterexample
543	  schedule at code level and assessing consequence — 98% of the violations
544	  it judges real, with reproduction a gate rather than an attempt. Polygraph
545	  stops at a spec-level counterexample path.
546	- **It guards its own repairs.** When a spec is repaired to pass trace
547	  validation, the repaired model is model-checked against *protocol-level*
548	  invariants — catching repairs that bought conformance by admitting illegal
549	  behavior. Polygraph's positive/negative controls prove the harness can
550	  tell a good spec from a mutated one; that is a check on the instrument,
551	  not on each repair. Different points, and we only have the one.
552	- **It triages, and publishes the split.** Of the violations that reach
553	  reproduction: 47.5% confirmed as real bugs, 48.8% discharged as *masked*
554	  with evidence — real invariant breaks with no observable consequence — and
555	  1.0% left unreproducible. Polygraph hands you all of them as leads to
556	  check by hand.
557	- **It has third-party confirmation.** Upstream maintainers confirmed 68 of
558	  its 89 reported findings and fixed 24. Polygraph has one corroborated
559	  production bug and a seeded-bug eval.
560	- **It requires invariants to cite their evidence** — a commit, code
561	  location, issue, or advisory, and it reports the distribution (code and
562	  comments back 87% of its invariants, issue trackers and pull requests
563	  74%, commit history 43%). polynv harvests candidates but does not demand
564	  provenance.
565	- **It is agent-agnostic.** Adapters ship for Claude Code, Codex, Copilot
566	  CLI, OpenCode and Pi, and any phase can be routed to a different agent or
567	  model. Polygraph's generation steps shell out to `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`.
568	
569	The difference is not that Polygraph audits better. It is that auditing is
570	one engine of several here, and Specula has **no authoring, no CI gate, no
571	runtime, and no versioning** — its paper states specs are generated from a
572	snapshot and must be regenerated when the code changes. Its evaluation ran
573	on a 96-core, 384 GB machine driving Opus-4.8 at 1M context and maximum
574	reasoning; a single CometBFT module took 670 agent steps and 1.9 billion
575	generated states. At a median of $57 and 3.7 hours per system — 5–37× the
576	token cost of an unaided agent — it structurally cannot run on every merge
577	request; Polygraph's model check and replay are keyless and deterministic,
578	which is what makes `polygate` possible. Different bet, different slot. If
579	your problem is deep bugs in a large concurrent or distributed system
580	written in C, C#, C++, Erlang, Go, Java, or Rust, **use Specula** — that is
581	what it is for, and it is good at it.

601	
602	<p align="center">
603	  <img src="assets/polygraph-architecture.png" alt="Polygraph architecture — one deterministic gate at the center, founded on SAM v2: polygen/polynv/polyvers author, elicit, and evolve the machine at design time; polyrun executes it durably at runtime; polysec and polyman prove and enforce policy for agents; SysMoBench qualifies SAM v2 across models; 100 production state machines tune the toolset" width="900">

605	
606	Everything revolves around three artifacts you can read and diff:
607	
608	1. **A contract** (`contract.json`) — what's observable: the state fields
609	   that matter, the actions the machine accepts, the data each action can
610	   carry, which states are terminal. This is the scope of the audit.
611	
612	2. **A spec** — an executable model of your code, written by an LLM from your
613	   source. By default it's a strict, self-describing state-machine module
614	   (the [SAM pattern](https://sam.js.org) v2 strict profile): every action it
615	   ignores must say *why* (`reject(reason)`), it can't hide bookkeeping
616	   state, and it declares its own action/data domains — so the model checker
617	   knows exactly what to explore with zero configuration. Several specs are
618	   generated independently and vote, so one bad generation doesn't decide the
619	   outcome.
620	
621	3. **Invariants** (`invariants.mjs`) — your rules, as plain JS functions over
622	   a state: *"never charged without a confirmed transaction"*, *"an expired
623	   session can't accept input."* These encode your **intent**, which is the
624	   one thing no tool can derive from the code — code with a bug is a faithful
625	   description of the wrong behavior.
626	
627	Then two checks run:
628	
629	**Check 1 — replay (is the spec faithful?).** Real execution traces —
630	captured by wrapping your dispatch/reducer once, so every step logs a
631	`{pre, action, data, post}` window — are replayed against each spec. Before
632	any generated spec is trusted, controls run: a hand-written reference spec
633	must score 100% and a deliberately mutated one must fail, proving the harness
634	can actually tell good from bad. Disagreements are triaged into
635	**spec-errors** (the LLM misread the code), **code-findings** (the code
636	disagrees with an independent reading of itself — investigate), and
637	**contract-errors** (the contract mis-scoped the problem).
638	
639	**Check 2 — model check (where the bugs are).** The faithful spec is iterated
640	exhaustively from its initial state against your invariants. This is the step
641	that finds what tests miss: replay can only flag a bug when spec and code
642	*disagree*, and a faithful spec reproduces the bug right along with the code.
643	Model checking reaches the bad state anyway and prints the shortest path to
644	it. Every check also runs a determinism double-pass for free.
645	
646	### What "exhaustive" means — and what it doesn't
647	
648	The checker enumerates a **finite (action, data) domain** declared in the
649	contract (or inferred from traces) and visits every state reachable from
650	`init` over that domain. So the precise coverage claim is: **state machines
651	expressible in the SAM v2 strict profile with finite declared domains** —
652	control-dominated logic (order workflows, auth lockouts, approval flows)
653	whose data can be finitized to representative values. It is *not* "arbitrary
654	state machines": a machine whose behavior depends on unbounded counters,
655	amounts, or strings is checked only at the representative values someone
656	declared. Finitizing data this way is the classic, defensible modeling move —
657	it is exactly what TLA+ users do with model bounds — but the abstraction gap
658	between the declared domain and real data is where bugs can hide, and **no
659	current gate measures that gap**. Choosing domain values that exercise every
660	boundary the code branches on (and re-checking the contract when the code
661	grows a new branch) is human judgment, on the same footing as writing the
662	invariants. One mitigation is built in: the domain cross-check that catches
663	contract/code vocabulary mismatches
664	([`examples/case-study-polygen-domain-gap.md`](examples/case-study-polygen-domain-gap.md))
665	— but it checks *spelling agreement*, not *representativeness*. The other
666	half of the judgment — whether the invariants you wrote are *strong* — now
667	has a partial measure: polynv's mutation adequacy grade
668	([`polynv/README.md`](polynv/README.md)) reports how many behaviorally
669	distinct machine mutations your rule set kills, with its own blind spot
670	stated (behavior-*removing* mutations largely evade safety invariants).
671	The domain-representativeness gap itself remains unmeasured.
672	
673	**polygen** runs the same machinery in reverse: draft contract → author
674	module → propose invariants → model-check → self-repair on violations (capped
675	at `--repair-max` rounds; a non-converging run is reported as NOT converged,
676	never silently presented as clean) → synthesize and independently replay a
677	trace corpus. It also cross-checks that contract and code agree on their
678	action/data vocabulary, because the two come from independent model calls —
679	[`examples/case-study-polygen-domain-gap.md`](examples/case-study-polygen-domain-gap.md)
680	shows a real run where a silent enum-spelling mismatch collapsed the
681	explorable state space, and how the check caught it.
682	
683	polygen output is JS/TS only: the generated module is directly usable in a
684	JS/TS codebase; porting a verified model to another language would need its
685	own differential check and is out of scope.

687	## Effort and prerequisites
688	
689	| step | who does it | how long |
690	|---|---|---|
691	| Define the contract (observable fields, actions, terminals) | you, or Claude drafts it for your review | minutes |
692	| Capture traces (instrument a copy, drive scenarios) | **the agent, in Claude Code** — it builds test doubles/emulators if needed; standalone, you wrap your dispatch once (snippet below) | the bulk of the work standalone; delegated in Claude Code |
693	| Write invariants (your rules as JS predicates) | you — this is your intent; the tool can propose, only you can confirm | minutes per rule |
694	| Generate specs, replay, model-check | automatic | minutes |
695	| Triage findings | you — every finding is a lead, not a verdict | depends on what it finds |
696	
697	Trace capture is historically what made this kind of verification expensive,
698	and it's the step the agent now carries: in the origin study, a Claude agent
699	built a payment-terminal emulator and a fault-injection proxy, instrumented a
700	production payment workflow, drove 17 scenarios, and produced a 75-window
701	corpus autonomously. What stays with you is judgment: confirming the contract
702	covers the right state, and sanity-checking any doubles the agent built
703	against reality.
704	
705	One hard prerequisite: **the code must be runnable in isolation**, because
706	traces are ground truth captured from the code actually executing. If it has
707	a clean step boundary (a dispatch, reducer, or handler), you're set. If it
708	only runs against a DB/network/device, stand up doubles first (or let the
709	agent do it). If it can't run at all, replay degenerates to checking specs
710	against your *expectations*, which can't find code bugs.
711	
712	Wrapping the boundary standalone is one line per scenario:
713	
714	```js
715	import { withTracing } from '<plugin>/scripts/instrument/trace-emitter.mjs';
716	
717	// project ONLY the contract's observable keys:
718	const project = () => ({ txState: m.txState, orderId: m.orderId });
719	const dispatch = withTracing(rawDispatch, project, 'traces/s1_normal.ndjson');
720	// Redux-style reducer: tapReducer(...)  ·  SAM component: withSamTracing(...) — see scripts/instrument/
721	```
